description: Viorel-powered team aimed at solving problem for all Viorels in the world
summary:
What we developed:

A harmonized fire record, and a web app to explore it. Each record reads as if one satellite had watched the whole time.
For the years before VIIRS, “virtual VIIRS” looks again at Aqua’s raw MODIS images. For every pixel it reconstructs what the ground and atmosphere would look like without fire, treats the leftover heat as fire, and converts it into the fires VIIRS would have reported.
For recent years, “virtual Aqua” converts VIIRS images to MODIS’s wavelengths, orbit and pixel shape, then runs the MODIS fire algorithm.
The Burning Activity Calendar lets anyone draw an area and see its fire history as a calendar, timeline and animated heatmap.
Together, this gives continuous datasets at both VIIRS and MODIS standards, and the tools to analyze them.
details:
1. Virtual VIIRS: the fires MODIS left out (2002 to 2012). MODIS's own fire list keeps only the obvious fires. We go back to its raw images, rebuild what every pixel would look like without fire, and treat the leftover heat as fire, including faint fires that were never reported. At night, MODIS's product flags about 1 in 20 of the pixels where VIIRS sees fire; our method finds about two thirds. A model learned from the overlap years then writes them down as the fires VIIRS would have listed.

2. Virtual Aqua: an on-time Aqua after the drift. We take VIIRS's sharp images, convert them into MODIS's wavelengths, blur them into MODIS's big pixels on an on-time Aqua orbit, and run MODIS's own fire algorithm. The result is what Aqua would see today if it had never drifted.

3. One record, no jump. Real and virtual pieces join, giving one record at VIIRS standard and one at MODIS standard. Striped means translated, and both switch points (2012 and 2022) are checked for jumps.

4. The Burning Activity Calendar. Pick or draw an area and see every month since 2002 as a calendar cell, with unusual months marked, a timeline against the usual range, a trend over the years, an animated heatmap, and downloads. Every page labels what is real observation and what is a converted estimate. Answers come back in under a second.


Available download formats

Monthly totals (ZIP): fire activity for each month, with its uncertainty range and flags. The flags mark converted estimates, partly covered months and missing data.

Raw hotspot points (CSV): the underlying detections, with a column saying where each row comes from. Real satellite months give one row per detected fire. Virtual months give one row per 0.25° cell with its fire count. Very large requests (over about 1 million points) are refused, with a prompt to choose a shorter period.

Animated heatmap (GIF): the selected period played month by month on a fixed colour scale, with annotations.

Calendar image (PNG): the whole-record calendar as a picture, ready for a report or slide.

Does it work?

We taught the translators on 2012 to 2021, when both satellites flew, and checked them on data they never saw.

- Virtual Aqua: across 40 unseen scene pairs, its fire energy is within about 1% of real Aqua.

- Virtual VIIRS, Madagascar: yearly totals agree with real VIIRS within about 2% in most years. In 2022, a year kept hidden until the end, the gap was 1.7%.

- Night: results at night are looser, and the app says so.

Benefits and intended impact

- Trends you can trust: emissions modellers, climate researchers, fire agencies and journalists can compare 2005 with 2025 directly, without a false jump at 2012.

- More history from old data: fires that sat unreported in the MODIS archive for 20 years are recovered.

- A record with a future: MODIS ends in 2027 and S-NPP ended in November 2026. The method works with the NOAA-20 and NOAA-21 VIIRS instruments that remain.

Why it is creative

Most harmonization multiplies one sensor's counts by a factor. We rebuild the images instead, in both directions. That recovers fire signal no one had extracted, and it rebuilds a satellite as if its orbit had never drifted.

Factors we considered

- All eight sensor differences shown above, not just pixel size.

- Fair testing: rules were fixed before the results, and test data was kept unseen.

- Honesty: every value carries a range and flags, and empty is never shown as zero.

- Cost: a full ten-year region costs a few dollars of cloud compute.

- Scope: built first for Madagascar. A global run is the next step.

Tools

- Science: Python (NumPy, SciPy, scikit-learn, pandas, pyhdf, netCDF4).

- Data: NASA LAADS DAAC, NASA FIRMS, ERA5, MODIS burned area, Microsoft Planetary Computer.

- Cloud: Microsoft Azure (VMs, Blob Storage, Container Apps).

- Backend: FastAPI, DuckDB, Parquet, OpenAPI.

- Frontend: React, TypeScript, Vite, Vitest.
